A bruise is a dark, discolored patch that appears on the surface of something — most often human skin — after it has been hit or struck hard, without the surface being cut open or broken.

Think of it this way: when something hits you hard enough to hurt, but not hard enough to break your skin, a bruise is what gets left behind.

To truly understand a bruise, you need to understand what happens beneath the surface.

Your skin is like a covering over a vast network of tiny blood vessels called capillaries. These are extremely thin, fragile tubes that carry blood throughout your body.

When you are hit by something — say, you bang your knee against a table — the force of the impact travels through your skin and damages these small blood vessels underneath. They crack or burst. Blood leaks out of them and into the surrounding tissue (the soft material under your skin).

Here is the key point: your skin has not been cut, so this leaked blood has nowhere to escape. It stays trapped under your skin, pooling in one place. It is this pool of blood sitting under your skin that you see as a bruise.
What a Bruise Looks, Feels, and Acts Like

Color: A bruise is not always the same color. It goes through a series of color changes as it heals, because the blood trapped under your skin gradually breaks down:

  • Right after the injury: It may look red or pinkish, since the blood is fresh.
  • Within a day or two: It darkens into blue, purple, or almost black. This is the stage most people recognize as a bruise.
  • As it heals: It fades to green, then yellow, then disappears entirely as your body reabsorbs the blood.

Feel: A bruise is almost always tender — meaning it hurts or aches when you press on it, even gently. The area may also feel slightly swollen or raised.

Size and shape: Bruises can range from a tiny dot to a large patch covering several inches of skin. The harder or more forceful the blow, the larger and darker the bruise tends to be.

Healing: Bruises heal on their own. No blood escapes the body — your body simply breaks down and reabsorbs the leaked blood over time. A typical bruise disappears within two to four weeks.

The word "bruise" (as a noun) is used in a few distinct but related ways:

1. A skin bruise — the most common meaning. Exactly as described above: a discolored, tender patch on your skin from a bump or blow. Also called a contusion in medical language.

2. A bone bruise — when the force of an impact damages the tissue inside a bone without actually cracking or breaking the bone. You cannot see it from the outside, but it causes deep, persistent pain. It is more serious than a skin bruise.

3. An internal bruise (internal bleeding / hematoma) — sometimes a bruise forms deep inside the body, around organs, where it cannot be seen at all. This is medically more serious, since a large amount of blood can pool internally. A hematoma is a specific medical word for a significant collection of blood under the skin or inside the body.

4. A bruise on fruit or vegetables — when an apple, banana, or other soft fruit is knocked, dropped, or squeezed too hard, it develops a soft, brown, mushy, discolored spot. This is also called a bruise. The tissue of the fruit has been damaged, just as body tissue is damaged in a human bruise.

5. A figurative bruise — in everyday language, people sometimes use "bruise" to describe emotional hurt. For example: "That harsh criticism left a bruise on his confidence." Here, it means a wound to someone's feelings, pride, or self-esteem — something that hurt and left a lasting mark, even if not a physical one.

• Contusion — the formal medical term for a bruise on the body. Means exactly the same thing.
  • Hematoma — a more severe form where blood collects in a distinct pocket or lump under the skin or inside the body.
  • Black and blue — a common phrase used to describe the appearance of a heavily bruised area.
  • Tender — how a bruise feels when touched; sore but not from a cut.

A bruise is the visible, painful mark left on skin (or deep inside the body) when a blow damages blood vessels beneath the surface without cutting it open. The dark color comes from blood that leaked out of those vessels and got trapped under the skin. It hurts when pressed, changes color as it heals, and eventually disappears on its own. The word can also describe similar damage to fruit, or emotional damage to a person's pride or feelings.
